questions.q: What did the Instance Health Dashboard show in this lab's scenario, and what did that combination indicate?
options: Response time roughly tripled while transaction volume stayed flat — indicating genuine degradation, not just a busier-than-usual day
Response time stayed flat while transaction volume tripled, indicating normal busy-Tuesday traffic
Both response time and transaction volume dropped to zero, indicating a full outage
Instance Health showed no data at all during the incident window
questions.explain: Rising response time with flat volume is exactly the 'something degraded' signal from Lesson 19, confirming scope as genuinely instance-wide.

questions.q: What deployment detail made the Business Rule the likely root cause rather than a coincidence?
options: It only affected a single, rarely-used custom table
It deployed just three minutes before the first reports, and it ran an unindexed GlideRecord query on every update to a heavily-used table
It was deployed a full week before the incident with no timing correlation
It was a cosmetic UI change with no server-side query logic
questions.explain: Strong timing correlation plus a plausible, specific mechanism (an unindexed query running constantly on a high-traffic table) made this the likely root cause, not just a guess.

questions.q: Why was elevated semaphore usage in this scenario treated as a downstream effect rather than a separate, competing cause?
options: Slower transactions naturally hold semaphores longer, which follows from the Business Rule's query slowness rather than indicating an independent problem like a runaway job
Semaphore usage was actually completely normal throughout the incident
Semaphore usage is never related to transaction duration in any way
There was clear evidence of a separate runaway scheduled job causing it
questions.explain: With no sign of a runaway job or separate capacity event, elevated semaphore usage was consistent with the Business Rule theory, not a second independent cause.

questions.q: Why did this incident NOT need a ServiceNow Support case?
options: Support cases are only for cosmetic issues, never performance problems
The incident resolved on its own before anyone could investigate it
It was a customization-caused problem that was fully self-diagnosable and self-fixable, not a genuine platform or infrastructure issue
ServiceNow Support cases are never needed for any platform-wide slowdown
questions.explain: Lesson 20's dividing line applies cleanly here: an unoptimized Business Rule the customer's own team wrote and could fix is on the customer's side of the line.

questions.q: What made this lab's prevention action specific enough to actually work, per the postmortem written for it?
options: It named a concrete automated check (flagging unindexed Business Rule queries on high-volume tables in the ATF suite), with an owner and a deadline before the next release
It assigned blame to the specific developer who wrote the rule
It simply stated that developers would be more careful with future Business Rules
It recommended disabling all Business Rules platform-wide permanently
questions.explain: A named change, a named owner, and a real deadline are what separate a working prevention action from a vague intention, per Lesson 21.
